title: When sharers become correctors: Exploring self-corrected debunking in a pandemic context
screen_reason: The paper's aim is psychological (what predicts self-corrected debunking), but its sample description reports descriptive shares of respondents who SHARED misinformation, which the eligibility rule includes explicitly. A naturalistic online survey of 1,317 Chinese adults on 14 February 2020 asked whether they had accidentally shared misinformation since the outbreak, then had them tick which of 12 fact-checked-false COVID-19 claims they had shared. 83.00% of the full sample had shared misinformation; 745/1,317 (56.6%) said so unprompted. Both are RECALL-sharing estimates with a stated denominator. The debunking outcomes are intentions/actions about CORRECTION and are out of scope.

estimates.platform: Not specified - sharing 'with their family or friends'; the 12 misinformation items were trending on Weibo at the time
estimates.date: 14 February 2020 (single-day collection, early stage of the COVID-19 outbreak); recall window is 'since the outbreak of the pandemic'
estimates.measure_type: % of respondents who had shared COVID-19 misinformation since the outbreak - either admitted unprompted, or revealed by ticking at least one of 12 fact-checked-false claims
estimates.value_raw: 83.00% of the full sample of 1,317 (Table 1: Group I n = 745 self-reported sharers + Group II n = 348 newly aware sharers = 1,093)
estimates.denominator: 1,317 Chinese adults recruited on the Credamo crowdsourcing platform (1,361 recruited, 44 excluded for failing attention checks); mean age 29.32, 705 male / 612 female, 73.58% with or reading for a bachelor's degree
estimates.definition: Counted if the respondent either answered yes to 'Have you accidently shared misinformation since the outbreak of the pandemic?' (Group I, n = 745) or answered no but then selected one or more of the 12 listed COVID-19 misinformation items as something they had shared (Group II, n = 348). Crucially, respondents ticked the items BEFORE being told they were false, so the prompted branch does not depend on the respondent recognising the claim as misinformation.
estimates.misinfo_def: No abstract definition; the construct is operationalised by the item set: "All 12 pieces of misinformation used in the shared-information selection task (e.g., 'Don't play in the snow. It will cause COVID-19 infection.') were collected from Chinese mainstream media and were trending on Weibo (www.weibo.com), one of the largest social media platforms in China, during the data collection period. The corresponding debunking information was sourced from authoritative Chinese fact-checking websites, including Tencent Fact Check and Dingxiang Yisheng."
estimates.source_quote: Across the fullsample, 83.00% of participants reported having shared misinformation at some point since the outbreak of COVID-19.
estimates.page_loc: Results, Section 3.2 'Descriptive statistics', p. 4, with Table 1 'Number of participants categorized by misinformation sharing experiences'
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Coded self_report per the RECALL convention - the sharing act is self-reported throughout and never verified against platform data. The falsity side is nevertheless externally anchored for most of the numerator: the 12 claims were verified false against authoritative Chinese fact-checking sources (Tencent Fact Check, Dingxiang Yisheng), so for the 1,047 respondents whose sharing was established by ticking a listed item the veracity ground truth is external, while the 46 Group I respondents who said yes but ticked none of the 12 rest on their own designation.
estimates.moderator_quote: The data for this study were collected at the onset of the COVID-19 outbreak on February 14, 2020. We recruited 1,361 participants through Credamo (www.credamo.com), a widely used crowdsource platform in China. After excluding 44 participants who failed the attention checks, the final sample consisted of 1,317 participants
estimates.notes: This 83.00% is a prompted-recognition measure and is unusually high for a self-reported sharing figure precisely because of the design: respondents were shown a checklist of 12 specific claims that were trending on Weibo that week and asked which they had shared, before being told any of them were false. That removes the social-desirability barrier that depresses ordinary 'did you share fake news?' items, but it also anchors on a dozen claims chosen for being ubiquitous, so it is a ceiling-flavoured estimate of sharing during one intense fortnight of a national health emergency, not a general-purpose misinformation-sharing rate. 83.00% x 1,317 = 1,093.1, matching 745 + 348 exactly. Non-probability paid online panel, skewed young (mean 29.3) and educated (73.6% degree-level). The source_quote reproduces the PDF text's missing space in 'fullsample' verbatim.

estimates.platform: Not specified - sharing 'with their family or friends'; the 12 misinformation items were trending on Weibo at the time
estimates.date: 14 February 2020 (single-day collection, early stage of the COVID-19 outbreak); recall window is 'since the outbreak of the pandemic'
estimates.measure_type: % of respondents who, unprompted, said yes to having accidentally shared misinformation since the outbreak of the pandemic
estimates.value_raw: 745/1,317 (Group I n = 745 of the final sample of 1,317)
estimates.denominator: 1,317 Chinese adults recruited on the Credamo crowdsourcing platform, after excluding 44 who failed attention checks
estimates.definition: Answered 'yes' to the single unaided item 'Have you accidently shared misinformation since the outbreak of the pandemic?', asked before any list of claims was shown; respondents supplied their own notion of what counted as misinformation
estimates.misinfo_def: No abstract definition; for this item the respondent's own understanding of 'misinformation' governs, since the 12 fact-checked claims were only presented afterwards
estimates.source_quote: Participants who reported having shared misinformation during the pandemic were categorized as Group I (n = 745).
estimates.page_loc: Results, Section 3.2 and Table 1, p. 4; Participants, Section 2.2, p. 3
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Group I membership is defined purely by the respondent's own yes/no answer, given before the 12 fact-checked items were shown; nothing external validates either the sharing or the falsity at this point. (699 of the 745 subsequently ticked a listed item, which corroborates most of them after the fact, but that is not how the group was constituted.)
estimates.moderator_quote: Those who answered "yes" to the question, "Have you accidently shared misinformation since the outbreak of the pandemic?" were classified as prior misinformation sharers (Group I individuals). Participants who answered "no" to this question but selected one or more misinformation items from our list (i.e., did not choose "shared none of the information above") were classified as newly aware misinformation sharers (Group II individuals).
estimates.notes: definition_variant=true: the narrower, unaided version of the same measure on the same denominator as the 83.00% row. The pair is the point of extracting both - unaided self-report gives 56.6%, prompted recognition against a checklist of 12 verified-false claims gives 83.00% on the identical sample. That 26-point gap is a clean within-study estimate of how much question format alone moves a self-reported sharing rate, which is exactly the methodological lever this review codes. Computed as an exact part/whole from two verbatim counts with the same denominator (745/1,317 = 56.57%), permitted under R8; the paper never prints the percentage itself.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: (1) Group II alone (n = 348, 26.4%) - the respondents who denied sharing but ticked a listed item. It is interesting (a direct measure of unaware sharing) but as a standalone share it is the difference between the two rows above, and reporting all three would triple-count the same 1,093 people. (2) Group III / misinformation-free (n = 224, 17.0%) - the complement of the 83.00% row, and R8 forbids keeping a complement. (3) 699 + 348 = 1,047 (79.5%) who ticked at least one listed item - a cross-category sum of two Table 1 cells that I would have to compute, barred by R8, even though it is arguably the cleanest fact-check-anchored sharing rate in the paper. (4) All debunking outcomes: Group I's binary debunking action, Group II's and Group III's debunking intentions, and every regression coefficient - these are correction behaviours and, for Group III, explicitly hypothetical ('asked to imagine a hypothetical situation'), which the protocol excludes. (5) Perceived veracity of the debunking information (5-point scale), trait empathy and apology scores - psychological scales, no share. (6) The number of misinformation pieces shared is used as a regression control but no mean is printed, so no per-capita intensity row is possible. One genuine uncertainty: the sentence 'Across the full sample, 83.00% of participants reported having shared misinformation' is loose, since 348 of those 1,093 did NOT report sharing misinformation - they reported sharing items the researchers then revealed to be misinformation. I have coded the row to the arithmetic (745 + 348 = 1,093 = 83.00% of 1,317), which is what the number is, and spelled the distinction out in the definition field.

rob.design: Cross-sectional naturalistic online survey, single day (14 February 2020), at the height of China's first COVID-19 wave. Non-probability convenience sample from the Credamo paid crowdsourcing platform: 1,361 recruited, 44 removed for failed attention checks, 1,317 analysed; 4.5 RMB compensation; ethics approval from Peking University; data and code open at https://osf.io/e5a3n. Exposure measure is a two-stage self-report - an unaided yes/no about accidental misinformation sharing, then a checklist of 12 COVID-19 claims trending on Weibo, with falsity established from Tencent Fact Check and Dingxiang Yisheng and disclosed to participants only after they had made their selections. No verification of any reported sharing against platform data. Sample skews young (M = 29.32, SD = 6.94) and highly educated (73.58% degree-level), so it is not representative of the Chinese population. Scale reliabilities are reported for the psychological measures (e.g. apology tendency alpha = .89, self-blame inter-item r = .25-.43) but there is no reliability statistic for the sharing measure, which is a single item plus a checklist. Materials were developed in Chinese and translated for reporting.
